**Audience**: an engineer who deploys ML and hits distribution, federated learning, robustness. **Empirical first**: FedAvg that stalls as soon as 3 clients are Byzantine; DP-SGD that costs −6 accuracy points for ε=8; then we name robust aggregation, DP composition, scaling.

Distributed / federated learning, Byzantine robustness, privacy — the systems view of LLMs (CMAP).

### What you will be able to do

-   Analyze distributed stochastic gradient descent: convergence speed, the effect of mini-batch size, step size, and number of workers.
-   Distinguish distributed learning architectures (centralized, local, federated) and their communication/computation trade-offs.
-   Explain the federated learning model (FedAvg) and its assumptions, in particular data heterogeneity across clients.
-   Identify Byzantine failures in a learning cluster and apply the robust aggregation rules that neutralize them.
-   Define differential privacy (ε-differential privacy), apply it to SGD, and interpret the utility/privacy trade-off.
-   Reason about collaboration challenges: per-client personalization, fairness across participants, incentives.
-   Estimate the cost of a training run (scaling models and compute) and read the scaling laws that structure the field (self-study).
-   Turn a theme of collaborative learning into a well-posed research question, and work on it in a group up to a presented and written research project.
-   Read a research paper in three passes and write a critique of it: claim, assumptions, evidence, scope, next question.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

**Official objectives**: the 2026-2027 SynapseS sheet of the course unit (APM_51178_EP, "EA Collaborative Learning") now displays a short description.

In paraphrase: the course explores collaborative learning *through a scientific approach* and teaches students to *formulate their own research questions*; the class first studies together the foundations of several themes, then students carry out *group activities* around these questions; finally, *three sessions are devoted to reading scientific articles*, to learn how to read them and how to take a critical view of their content.

The sheet names neither the themes nor a session-by-session programme, and displays no separate objectives list. The only assessment text it shows (in the section of the MScT IoT track; the LLGA section is empty) is that the final grade is based on the **presentation and the report of the research project** prepared during the course unit; the recommended prerequisite (MAP433) is stated for the engineering cycle only.

The title and its history ("Emerging Topics in Machine Learning - Collaborative Learning" in 2025-2026, under the Dieuleveut & El Mhamdi team as recorded earlier on this site) designate the field: *collaborative* learning — learning together when data, computation and participants are distributed, heterogeneous and mutually distrustful.

### Where this course fits in the program

Recommended option of the LLGA track in Year 1 · Period 1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS). The official sheet recommends MAP433 for students of the engineering cycle; in practice, this module assumes the optimization foundation of the [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) module, whose opening chapter covers the analysis of SGD — extended here to the distributed case — and the theory of generalization.

The two refreshers ([Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html), [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html)) are its upstream prerequisites. The course unit is shared with the engineering cycle (X), the MJH master, exchange programs, the MScT Visual Computing and Creative AI track, and (according to the assessment sections of the sheet) the MScT IoT and TRAI tracks.

Downstream, this module opens three directions. [Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html) (M2) extends the differential privacy seen here toward private inference and uncertainty quantification; [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (M2) picks up scaling and the systems viewpoint for industrializing LLMs; [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (Period 2) draws on the same questions of collaboration and multiple agents, up to multi-agent RL.

### Course outline

-   **Review: SGD and its analysis**: convergence of stochastic gradient descent, taken from the Machine Learning module and extended to distributed systems.
-   **Landscape of emerging topics**: a map of the research fronts that structure large-scale ML today, and how to turn one of them into a research question of your own.
-   **Distributed learning**: parallelizing training, synchronizing workers, arbitrating between communication and computation.
-   **Federated learning**: learning on data that never leaves its owners — the FedAvg framework and its variants.
-   **Byzantine robustness**: detecting and tolerating faulty or malicious workers in aggregation.
-   **Differential privacy**: formalizing and guaranteeing the protection of individuals during training.
-   **Collaboration, personalization, fairness**: learning models together that remain useful to everyone — and fair.
-   **Scaling and compute**: what large models cost, and what the field's scaling laws say.
-   **Course research notes — CMAP (El Mhamdi, Dieuleveut)**: the research of El Mahdi El Mhamdi (Byzantine robustness) and Aymeric Dieuleveut (stochastic SGD, federated learning), CMAP, and a method for reading papers critically — the material of the three official paper-reading sessions (the 2026-2027 coordinator is Paul Mangold).

### Session plan {#sessions}

**36 h in class = 12 sessions of 3 h.** The volume is the one of the SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet (36 h in person, lecture/tutorial/lab split not displayed). The sheet gives no session-by-session programme, but it does fix the structure, and the plan follows it: foundations of several themes studied together, with group work on research questions (sessions 1 to 9), *then* three sessions devoted to reading scientific articles (sessions 10 to 12).

To make room for those three sessions, the scaling chapter (ch. 7), which the sheet does not name, moves to self-study, and distributed learning (ch. 2) and Byzantine robustness (ch. 4) take one session each.

Level 1 = foundations (reviews, definitions, first worked examples, framing a research question), 2 = core methods (the distributed, federated, robust and private algorithms with their guarantees), 3 = research material (reading and criticizing the papers that founded these methods); the level never goes down from one session to the next.
